lessons.title: From notebook to script
key_points: A notebook is good for exploring but hard to rerun: cells can run out of order and hidden state builds up. Deployable code lives in plain .py files that run top to bottom.
Split the work into a training script (train.py: load data, fit, save the model) and a prediction module (predict.py: load the model, predict).
Save the whole scikit-learn Pipeline with joblib.dump(pipe, "model.joblib"), so the same preparation steps run at prediction time.
Pin your library versions in requirements.txt (for example scikit-learn==1.5.2). A model saved with one version may not load in another.
Fix random seeds and log the data version and test score each time you train, so a model can be traced back to how it was made.

worked_example.title: Move the iris model out of a notebook
steps: Create train.py that loads the data, splits it, fits make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()) and prints the test score.
At the end of train.py, call joblib.dump(pipe, "model.joblib").
Create predict.py with a function predict(rows) that loads model.joblib once and returns pipe.predict(rows).
Run python train.py, then python -c "from predict import predict; print(predict([[5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]]))".
worked_example.code:
# train.py
import joblib
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("test accuracy", pipe.score(X_te, y_te))
joblib.dump(pipe, "model.joblib")

mini_project.title: Make your model rerunnable
mini_project.brief: Turn one of your notebook models into scripts.
steps: Write train.py that trains and saves your model in one run.
Write predict.py with a predict function that loads the saved model.
Create requirements.txt with pinned versions (pip freeze, then keep only what you use).
Delete the saved model, run train.py again and check the score is the same.
mini_project.done_when: A fresh python train.py recreates the model and predict.py uses it.

lessons.title: A simple prediction API
key_points: An API lets other programs use your model over HTTP. A client sends input as JSON in a POST request and gets the prediction back as JSON.
FastAPI is a small Python web framework. You declare the input shape with a Pydantic model, and FastAPI rejects badly formed input with a 422 error before your code runs.
Load the model once when the app starts, not on every request; loading is slow.
Add a GET /health endpoint that returns {"status": "ok"}, so hosting platforms can check the service is alive.
Run it locally with uvicorn app:app --reload and try it from the automatic docs page at /docs.

worked_example.title: Serve the iris model
steps: Define a Pydantic class Flower with four float fields.
Load model.joblib at the top of app.py.
Write POST /predict that turns the Flower into a row, calls model.predict and returns the class name.
Start uvicorn, open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs, send {"sepal_length": 5.1, "sepal_width": 3.5, "petal_length": 1.4, "petal_width": 0.2} and get {"species": "setosa"}.
Send a string instead of a number and see the 422 error that Pydantic returns.

mini_project.title: Put an API in front of your model
mini_project.brief: Serve the model you scripted in lesson 1.
steps: Write app.py with /health and /predict, using a Pydantic model for the input.
Run it with uvicorn and make three predictions from the /docs page.
Call it from a second program with Python requests or curl.
Add one check of your own (for example, refuse negative values) and return a clear error message.
mini_project.done_when: Another program gets predictions from your running API, and bad input gets a clear error.

lessons.title: Running it in the cloud
key_points: A container packages your code, the model file, Python and the libraries into one image, so it runs the same on your laptop and on a server. Docker builds it from a Dockerfile.
Keep the image small: start from a slim Python base image, install only requirements.txt, and copy only the files the app needs.
Settings that change between places (the port, a model path, an API key) come from environment variables, not from the code. Never bake secrets into the image.
Cloud container services (for example Google Cloud Run or AWS App Runner) take an image, run it behind HTTPS, and start more copies when traffic grows.
After deploying, call /health and one /predict request against the public address before telling anyone it works.

worked_example.title: A Dockerfile for the iris API
steps: Start FROM python:3.12-slim and set WORKDIR /app.
COPY requirements.txt first and pip install it, so Docker can reuse that layer when only your code changes.
COPY app.py and model.joblib.
Start uvicorn on 0.0.0.0 and the port given by the PORT environment variable (default 8000).
Build with docker build -t iris-api . and run with docker run -p 8000:8000 iris-api, then open /docs.
worked_example.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py model.joblib ./
CMD ["sh", "-c", "uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT:-8000}"]

mini_project.title: Ship your container
mini_project.brief: Run your API from a container, then from a server if you have access to one.
steps: Write a Dockerfile for your API and build the image.
Run it locally with docker run and test /health and /predict.
Move one setting (such as the model path) into an environment variable.
If you have a free cloud account, deploy the image and test the public URL; otherwise write the exact deploy steps you would follow.
mini_project.done_when: Your API runs from a container and answers /health and /predict.

lessons.title: Watching it after launch
key_points: A model can get worse after launch without any code change, because the real data drifts away from the training data (new kinds of questions, a new semester, a new user group).
Log every request's time, input summary, prediction and response time. Do not log personal data you do not need.
Watch simple numbers: error rate, response time, how often each class is predicted, and input ranges compared with the training data.
When true answers arrive later (for example a lecturer corrects the bot), compare them with the predictions to measure live accuracy.
Keep the previous model version so you can roll back quickly, and retrain on fresh data on a schedule or when the numbers move.

worked_example.title: Spot drift in the FAQ bot
steps: The bot classifies questions by module. In week 1, 30% of predictions are "Android Programming".
In week 6, that share falls to 5% and many questions get low confidence.
The logs show many new questions about a module that started mid-semester, which was not in the training data.
You label 50 of the new questions, retrain, compare the new model with the old one on the same held-out set, and deploy only if it is better. The old version stays ready for rollback.

mini_project.title: Add monitoring to your API
mini_project.brief: Give your API the minimum it needs to be looked after.
steps: Log each /predict call to a CSV or the console: timestamp, predicted class and response time in milliseconds.
Write a short script that reads the log and prints the count per predicted class and the average response time.
Send 20 test requests, including a few with unusual values, and run the script.
Write down one threshold that would make you investigate (for example, average response time above 500 ms).
mini_project.done_when: Your log and summary script work, and you have written one alert rule.

check.prompt: Why save the whole scikit-learn Pipeline instead of only the final model?

options.text: The same preparation steps, such as scaling, run again at prediction time
joblib cannot save models on their own

check.explanation: If you save only the model, new inputs reach it without the scaling or encoding it was trained with, and predictions go wrong.

check.prompt: In a FastAPI app, when should the model file be loaded?

options.text: Inside the /predict function, on every request

check.explanation: Loading a model is slow. Loading it once at start-up means each request only runs the prediction.

check.prompt: A client sends {"sepal_length": "long"} to your /predict endpoint, which uses a Pydantic model with float fields. What happens?

options.text: FastAPI returns a 422 error saying the input is invalid

check.explanation: Pydantic checks the input before your function runs, and FastAPI answers with a 422 validation error that names the bad field.

check.prompt: Where should an API key used by your service come from?

options.text: An environment variable set on the server

check.explanation: Secrets in code or images end up in Git or image registries. Environment variables are set where the service runs and stay out of the code.

check.prompt: The code has not changed, but live accuracy has dropped over two months. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The incoming data has drifted away from the training data

check.explanation: When real inputs change (new topics, new users), a model trained on older data gets worse. Monitoring inputs and predictions shows this early.

review_cards.front: Why pin library versions in requirements.txt?
review_cards.back: A model saved with one version may not load, or may behave differently, with another.
Returns a simple OK so hosting platforms and people can check the service is alive.

review_cards.front: Why put the API in a container?
review_cards.back: Code, model, Python and libraries travel together, so it runs the same everywhere.
Live inputs changing away from the training data, which makes a model worse without any code change.
